segments.title: Introduction to Big O notation in computer science

sub_topics.name: Introduction to the topic
sub_topics.description: Hey, what's going on everybody? It's your bro, hope you're doing well, and in this video I'm going to describe the very basics of Big O notation in, well, computer science.

sub_topics.name: Explanation of Big O notation
sub_topics.description: Oh yeah, Big O notation. So a common phrase used with Big O notation is, how code slows as data grows. It describes the performance of an algorithm as the amount of data increases. And really, this notation is machine independent. What we're really focusing on is the number of steps to complete an algorithm, because some machines are going to run certain algorithms faster than others.

key_points: Big O notation is used to describe the performance of an algorithm
It focuses on the number of steps to complete an algorithm

segments.title: Examples of Big O notation

sub_topics.name: Example of a function with O(n) complexity
sub_topics.description: Here's a more concrete example. I have a function named addup. We will add up to a certain number depending on what we pass in as an argument. The for loop within here will iterate once up to whatever number that n is, add i to sum, then return it. What if n was a large number like a million? Well, it's going to take just above a million steps to complete this function.

sub_topics.name: Example of a function with O(1) complexity
sub_topics.description: Now another way which we could write the same function is to take sum equals n times n plus 1 divided by 2. We will get the exact same sum. So if n was, let's say, a million, this is still only going to take a couple seconds. steps. Three steps, not a million steps. So this function is going to have a runtime complexity of O of one.

key_points: O(n) complexity means the algorithm takes linear time
O(1) complexity means the algorithm takes constant time
The input size does not affect the complexity of an O(1) algorithm

segments.title: Explanation of different runtime complexities

sub_topics.name: Explanation of O(1), O(log n), and O(n) complexities
sub_topics.description: Here's a graph that I made to represent the different runtime complexities. We have data on the x-axis represented by n. So data will increase as we go more to the right, and we have time on the y-axis. I did add an asterisk next to time because some of these times can vary depending on what machine you're using, so these can vary

sub_topics.name: Explanation of O(n log n), O(n^2), and O(n!) complexities
sub_topics.description: Next we have O of N log N, also known as quasi-linear time. This would include a quick sort, merge sort, and heap sort. We'll talk about these concepts in future videos. So for the most part, this is very similar to linear time. Unless we're working with a large data set, then anything using O of N log N is going to start to slow down when we work with larger data sets, hence this curve here.

key_points: The choice of algorithm depends on the size of the input data
